## Abstract

Perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAA) are a well-studied subclass of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). Some PFAA bioaccumulate in food webs, and fish consumption is an important vector of human exposure. However, mechanistic studies investigating the relative importance of branchial uptake, tissue partitioning, and renal excretion of PFAA in fish are limited. We developed a mechanistic toxicokinetic (TK) model to examine gill transport as a potential rate-limiting step for PFAA uptake and elimination in fish. The model simulates laboratory conditions and explicitly accounts for transport across the aqueous boundary layer (ABL) at the gill epithelial membrane and co-transport with dissolved organic carbon (DOC). Modeled bioconcentration factors (BCFs) for PFAA containing 4–10 perfluorinated carbons (ηpfc) agreed with laboratory data within one standard deviation of the median. BCFs were most sensitive to by tissue binding (normalized sensitivity coefficients [NSCs] across PFAA: 69% to 102%). Elimination half-lives were sensitive to both tissue binding (57% to 76%) and effective gill permeability (−30% to −96%). ABL thickness at the gill epithelial membrane, rather than the epithelial membrane itself, determines the diffusion barrier for short-chain PFAA (ηpfc < 6) and was the most sensitive parameter (97%) affecting elimination half-lives. The gills accounted for 5–47% of tissue-bound PFAA, driven by binding to proteins and partitioning to phospholipids. At an aqueous DOC concentrations of 100 mg L−1, modeled BCFs decreased by up to 22%. Together, these results suggest tissue binding and gill permeability are both important for PFAA bioconcentration, and that uptake and exchange are affected by flow-dependent transport across the ABL at the gill epithelial membrane.

## Environmental significance

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), particularly terminal perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAA), are widespread contaminants in freshwater ecosystems that represent an important dietary exposure pathway for humans. This study presents a mechanistic toxicokinetic model that simulates PFAA uptake, tissue partitioning and elimination. The model accounts for differences in tissue binding, gill-mediated transport, and renal elimination. The model suggests that tissue binding provides a reasonable proxy for PFAA bioconcentration, while gill exchange affects the rate at which steady state is approached and therefore controls elimination half-lives. The model can be used to adjust laboratory test setups to represent natural conditions, including flow conditions and dissolved organic carbon levels that regulate transport across the ABL at the gill epithelium.

## Introduction

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are fluorinated organic chemicals that have been produced in large quantities for use in industrial processes and consumer products.1–3 PFAS are widely detected in fish and shellfish, and consumption of contaminated seafood contributes to human and ecological health risks.3,4 Perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAA) are a well-studied subset of PFAS that include perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCA) and perfluoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSA) with varying perfluorinated carbon chain lengths (ηpfc).5 PFAA with ηpfc ≥ 6 primarily accumulate in fish blood and highly perfused tissues such as the liver and kidneys.6–8 Prior modeling studies have suggested that gill transport may be a rate-limiting step for PFAA uptake in fish.7 Here, we developed a toxicokinetic (TK) model for freshwater fish with an explicit gill compartment to evaluate the role of gill transport for PFAA uptake, accumulation and elimination.

Most regulatory bioaccumulation studies, including those following OECD Test Guideline 305,9 were designed for neutral hydrophobic chemicals that rapidly permeate fish gills through passive diffusion and accumulate predominantly in lipid-rich adipose tissue.10–13 Bioaccumulation is often approximated using lipid-normalized equilibrium partition coefficients that simulate contaminant bioconcentration.14 In contrast, PFAA are predominantly anionic at environmental pH and exhibit low membrane permeability.15,16 PFAA preferentially associate with albumin and other functional proteins as well as phospholipids,17,18 while showing negligible affinity for storage lipids and more limited affinity to structural proteins.18 Phospholipid and structural proteins are both important for determining tissue-specific accumulation19,20 and whole-body PFAA concentrations.21

Fish gills consist of bilaterally symmetrical filaments that form a countercurrent respiratory chamber. At the epithelial membrane, an unstirred aqueous boundary layer (ABL) develops, where slow laminar flow creates a diffusional barrier to uptake.22,23 The gill epithelium regulates uptake and depuration of gases and ions.24,25 For toxicants, transbranchial absorption is initiated by diffusion across the ABL. ABL thickness determines the resistance to solute permeability at the gill when it is driven by passive diffusion.26,27 Previous models for PFAA uptake across fish gills assumed diffusion resistance or impermeability of specific gill layers mediated by water flow and pH,10–12,28,29 but did not account for the influence of ABL thickness.

Simplified laboratory studies are often used to evaluate the bioconcentration potential of environmental contaminants under representative ecosystem conditions including the effects of varying dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations.30 Co-transport of PFAA with DOC across the ABL may facilitate uptake.31,32 Conversely, binding to DOC may reduce freely dissolved concentrations in water available for biological uptake, potentially lowering observed bioconcentration factors (BCFs).33–35 Lab testing guidelines27 specify DOC concentrations of 2–10 mg L−1, which is more limited than ranges observed in natural aquatic environments that can vary from 0.1 to over 300 mg L−1.36

The main objective of this work was to better understand how gill processes, including ABL thickness and co-transport with DOC, influence uptake and elimination in freshwater fish. Specifically, we aimed to determine whether gill exchange is a rate-limiting step, relative to internal tissue distribution and renal elimination. To do this, we leveraged prior modeling efforts14,29,37–39 and developed a two-compartment TK model (blood and tissues) that explicitly accounts for the gill membrane and boundary layer transport. Compared with previous models, our model retains the gill as the exchange barrier for freely dissolved PFAA between water and blood and resolves its effective permeability from ABL diffusion, gill epithelial membrane permeability, and DOC-mediated transport. Other compartments were simplified to focus on respiratory exchange, tissue distribution, and elimination. We assessed nine PFAA (sulfonic and carboxylic acids with ηpfc = 4 to 10) to investigate chain-length- and functional group-dependent patterns. We compared simulated elimination half-lives and BCFs to laboratory measurements to evaluate model performance8,40,41 and conducted a series of sensitivity analyses to quantify the relative importance of different parameters. This work provides insight into the importance of gill transport processes for PFAA accumulation in freshwater fish.

## Model theory & parameterization

### Model overview

We developed a two-compartment TK model for simulating PFAA bioconcentration in freshwater fish. The model includes separate blood and tissue compartments. The tissue compartment consolidates all extravascular organs and tissues (Fig. 1). Preliminary multicompartment simulations revealed equilibrium partitioning reasonably captures internal tissue distribution. The tissue compartment is assumed to be well-mixed for a small (∼8 g) model fish.42,43 The model specifies respiratory exchange at secondary gill lamellae, where PFAS transfer between water and blood is governed by permeability across the ABL and the gill epithelial membrane.29 Depuration is assumed to occur via renal elimination of the free blood concentration. Refinements relative to previous TK models7 include parameterization of: (1) the permeability of the gill epithelial membrane, (2) ABL diffusion, and (3) effects of DOC binding on both ABL transport and aqueous bioavailability.

### Effective gill transport

Modeled initial uptake of PFAA from water is driven by the concentration gradient between freely dissolved PFAA in water (Cfree,water) and the PFAA-free fish. The diffusive flux across the gill is governed by Pgill, which integrates resistance across both the ABL (PABL, cm s−1) and the gill epithelium (Pmem, cm s−1).2,41

To account for the dual role of DOC, the model incorporates DOC-mediated transport across the ABL and adjusts for the reduced free PFAA concentration in water. PABL is derived from (Dfree + DDOC × KDOC/w × CDOC) × xABL−1, where Dfree and DDOC are the aqueous diffusivities of freely dissolved PFAA and DOC in stagnant water (cm2 s−1), respectively, KDOC/w is the DOC–water partition coefficient for ionized PFAA using organic carbon (OC) as a surrogate (Lwater kgDOC−1), CDOC is the DOC concentration in water (kgDOC Lwater−1), and xABL is ABL thickness (cm). We assumed DOC consists of humic substances at concentrations ranging from 1 × 10−6 g mL−1 to 1 × 10−4 g mL−1.49 In addition to DOC-mediated transport, binding to DOC reduces Cfree,water, which is calculated by Cwater = Cfree,water + Cfree,water × KDOC/w × CDOC,45 where Cwater is the total PFAA concentration in the water (µg cm−3).

The model accounts for chemical diffusion distances across xABL and the gill epithelial membrane (xmem, cm). Simulations were conducted assuming a 45 L flow-through tank representative of typical laboratory exposure conditions. We set xABL depending on the bioaccumulation test setup: under flowing water at 5.8 cm s−1, xABL was set to 0.016 cm; under static conditions, we increased xABL to 0.082 cm.50

### Model parameterization

Modeled PFAA were selected based on data availability for model evaluation,8,40,41 including perfluorobutane sulfonic acid (PFBS, ηpfc = 4), perfluorohexane sulfonic acid (PFHxS, ηpfc = 6), and perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS, ηpfc = 8) as well as perfluorohexanoic acid (PFHxA, ηpfc = 5), perfluoroheptanoic acid (PFHpA, ηpfc = 6), perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA, ηpfc = 7), perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA, ηpfc = 8), perfluorodecanoic acid (PFDA, ηpfc = 9), and perfluoroundecanoic acid (PFUDA, ηpfc = 10). All modeled PFAA are strong acids with low pKa values (−0.17 to 2.50) and are assumed to be fully ionized at environmental and physiological pH ranges.2,15,51 Partition coefficients (K) reported here therefore describe ionized species and are equivalent to distribution coefficients. Renal elimination rates (ke) were derived from prior studies.7,29 Following the approach of Ng and Hungerbühler,29 missing renal clearance and reabsorption rates were estimated by linear extrapolation over the number of perfluorinated carbons, based on data from Weaver et al.52 Data for PFBS and PFHxA were not available, so we estimated rates from the mean values reported by Lau et al.53 Physicochemical model parameters for PFAA included in this study were derived from in vitro data and are summarized in Tables S2 and S3.

Fish physiological parameters were collected for an 8 g rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss). Data included tissue and biofluid volumes, protein and lipid contents, and gill membrane morphology. Up to six phases were considered in fish blood and tissues: neutral lipids, phospholipids, functional proteins, structural proteins, nonlipid organic matter, and water. When tissue composition data were unavailable for rainbow trout, values were extrapolated from Labeo rohita, a freshwater fish with comparable physiology.48

The model uses a 13 cm2 surface area for the water-facing membrane of the secondary lamellae (Agill, cm2).29 We estimated the surface area of other fish tissues (Atissue, cm2), including gill (71 cm2), liver (16 cm2), kidney (22 cm2), muscle (34 cm2), and adipose tissue (23 cm2) based on total capillary surface areas to reflect the distribution of PFAA via systemic blood flow.29xmem varies depending on fish species and region of diffusion. Therefore, values representative of gas-exchange regions were used, with an assumed total thickness of 1 to 3 µm.25 Further details on the parameterization of fish physiology are provided in Tables S4 and S5.

### Model fits and performance evaluation

We followed the statistical framework outlined by Martin et al.40 to compare simulated with experimental BCFs. The depuration rate constant (kd, per day) was derived by linear regression of the log-transformed decline in simulated fish concentrations during the depuration phase. The uptake rate constant (ku, L per L per day) was derived by iterative nonlinear regression of time-dependent Cfish during the uptake phase, fitting the kinetic rate equation after correcting for fish growth. To do so, Cfish–time curves were fitted to Cfish(t) = a × exp(−kd × t) during the depuration period and blobs/8450/13555787/4a5aa3c363f3/d6em00160b-t6.jpgcdnNEVER_LOAD during the uptake period, where blobs/8450/13555787/4ca3b04abf28/d6em00160b-t7.jpgcdnNEVER_LOAD is the mean concentration of PFAA in water. To represent different laboratory conditions, two exposure scenarios were simulated: (i) a standard laboratory test setting, in which a single initial PFAA spike was added to the water, accounting for depletion of Cfree,water over time due to sorption to DOC and uptake into the fish; and (ii) a modified test setting for flow-through water systems that mimics natural freshwater systems, in which Cfree,water was assumed to remain constant. Elimination half-lives were calculated as ln(2)/kd. Apparent BCFs were determined from laboratory simulations as ku/kd given the standard laboratory test setting. Aqueous-exposure BCFs (BCFaq.) were assumed equal to the apparent BCF at steady state37,54,55 and calculated as the ratio of total modeled PFAA concentration in fish to that in water (Cfish/Cwater) at the end of the 28-day uptake period given the modified laboratory test setting. We examined the influence of variability in experimental partition coefficients by performing Monte Carlo simulations (n = 10 000 iterations), sampling each coefficient from its distribution. Following Fischer et al.,56 values reported by multiple studies were combined by inverse-variance-weighted averaging, and log10-transformed coefficients were represented by normal distributions with means and standard deviations summarized in Tables S2 and S3.

Model performance was evaluated by comparing simulated BCFs to experimental data reported by Burkhard et al.8 and Martin et al.40 For each PFAA, we extracted the median and standard deviation of measured BCFs across relevant exposure conditions. In addition, we assessed model sensitivity to parameter uncertainty using normalized sensitivity coefficients (NSCs, %), calculated as NSC = (Δr/r) × (p/Δp) × 100, where r represents the modeled output (i.e., BCF or elimination half-life), and p the parameter perturbed by 1%. An NSC > 100% indicates that a relative change in model input results in a greater relative change in model output.57

We evaluated the influence of parameters involved in three key processes: (1) mass transfer from water to blood, (2) blood–tissue distribution, and (3) elimination from blood, on predicted BCF and elimination half-lives. All simulations were performed in R (version 4.4.1) using the deSolve package (version 1.40).58

## Results & discussion

### Model evaluation

Modeled log10 BCFs for nine PFAA largely reproduced empirical values for freshwater fish within one log10 unit from literature-reported medians (Fig. 2). All simulations reached steady state by day 28, with <3% change in total fish concentrations over the final 48 hours of the uptake phase. Steady-state BCFsaq estimated under the modified laboratory test setting (i.e., constant PFAA influx) increased across PFAA, with values of 0.92 ± 0.05 (95% CI = 0.83–1.0) for PFBS, 1.1 ± 0.04 (95% CI = 0.99–1.1) for PFHxA, 1.7 ± 0.04 (95% CI = 1.6–1.7) for PFHpA, 1.9 ± 0.05 (95% CI = 1.8–2.0) for PFOA, 2.2 ± 0.04 (95% CI = 2.1–2.2) for PFNA, 2.4 ± 0.04 (95% CI = 2.3–2.4) for PFHxS, 2.7 ± 0.06 (95% CI = 2.5–2.8) for PFOS, 2.7 ± 0.06 (95% CI = 2.5–2.8) for PFDA, and 2.8 ± 0.03 (95% CI = 2.7–2.9) for PFUDA.

Discrepancies between modeled and experimental values may result from simplified assumptions in the model, including respiratory-only uptake and the absence of fecal elimination, which could bias accumulation estimates upward and downward for short- and long-chain PFAA, respectively. Modeled water concentrations remained stable during the 12-day uptake phase and closely matched measured values for all PFAA as reported by Martin et al. (Fig. S2).40 Simulated blood concentrations were approximately two-fold higher than measured values for PFHxS (sim. mean on day 12: 0.20 vs. exp. mean on day 12: 0.089 µg mL−1) and PFOA (0.063 vs. 0.040 µg mL−1), but substantially underestimated PFOS (0.029 vs. 1.2 µg mL−1), PFDA (0.053 vs. 1.5 µg mL−1), and PFUDA (0.025 vs. 2.9 µg mL−1), corresponding to 41-, 28-, and 110-fold discrepancies, respectively. Long-chain PFAA (ηpfc ≥ 8) typically show higher bioaccumulation than ηpfc < 8 PFAA. These discrepancies appear to reflect the measured blood concentrations rather than the model structure. Within the experimental dataset, blood concentrations of PFOS, PFDA, and PFUDA exceed those of PFOA by 30- to 70-fold at comparable exposure concentrations, a gap larger than expected given that these compounds partition preferentially into phospholipid- and protein-rich tissues rather than remaining in blood. The resulting rank order of blood concentrations simulated by the TK model (PFHxS > PFOA > PFDA > PFOS > PFUDA) was instead consistent with more recent in vivo studies that reported higher blood burdens of PFHxS and PFOA compared to PFOS, irrespective of exposure route.59,60

### Sensitivity analysis

Sensitivity analyses indicate that modeled whole-body BCFs are primarily controlled by tissue–water partitioning, whereas gill exchange has a strong influence on elimination half-lives (Fig. 3). For BCFs (Fig. 3A), normalized sensitivity coefficients (NSCs) were highest for tissue binding (Ktissue/w), ranging from 69% for PFHxS (ηpfc = 6) to 102% for PFUDA (ηpfc = 10). This indicates that a 2-fold increase in Ktissue/w leads to a 69–102% increase in predicted BCFs. In contrast, BCFs were only moderately sensitive to gill permeability (Pgill), with NSCs up to 23% for PFUDA, but ≤10% for ηpfc ≤ 7 PFAA. Renal elimination (ke) had a minor influence on BCFs for short-chain PFAA (e.g., −2.4% for PFBS, −2.4% for PFHxA), and was negligible for compounds with ηpfc ≥ 7, with NSCs around zero. These patterns align with other fish TK models, where BCF increases as renal elimination slows while gill uptake remains unchanged. Stronger tissue binding slows redistribution and clearance, elevating the steady-state uptake-to-loss ratio.13 Experimental data similarly show that long-chain PFAS preferentially accumulate in tissues rich in phospholipids and proteins.19,20,61 These results suggest that gill uptake and tissue retention are more important drivers of experimental bioconcentration factors over 28-day uptake and depuration periods rather than renal clearance for the PFAA evaluated in this study.7

Elimination half-lives were primarily governed by gill exchange and tissue binding, with sensitivity patterns varying by chain length (Fig. 3B). NSCs for gill permeability (Pgill) ranged from −30% for PFDA (ηpfc = 9) to −96% for PFBS (ηpfc = 4), underscoring the important role of gill exchange in PFAA elimination. NSCs for tissue binding (Ktissue/w) were uniformly positive, ranging from 57% (PFDA) to 76% (PFOS). Rapid branchial exchange lowered the blood concentration and steepened the tissue-to-blood gradient, driving net redistribution of PFAA out of tissues. Stronger tissue binding opposed this by retaining PFAA in tissue. Elimination half-lives were therefore dominated by gill exchange for the shorter-chain PFAA and by tissue binding for long-chain PFAA (ηpfc ≥ 7). We found minimal influence of renal elimination on elimination half-lives for long-chain PFAA. This result aligns with trout analyses showing that adding a renal-elimination term improves agreement mainly for short-chain PFAA (ηpfc < 7). Respiratory (gill) elimination tends to be orders of magnitude greater than renal elimination for long-chain PFAA (ηpfc ≥ 7),7 which is similar to neutral persistent organic pollutants (POPs).7

To identify processes controlling Pgill, we analyzed the sensitivity of the gill model subcomponents. The ABL emerged as the dominant diffusional barrier. NSCs for ABL thickness (xABL) ranged from −2.1% for PFOA to −23% for PFUDA with respect to BCFs, and from +31% (PFDA) to +97% (PFBS) for half-lives. In contrast, gill membrane diffusion (Dmem), binding to gill membranes (Kmem/w), and gill membrane thickness (xmem) mostly had NSCs below ±0.01%. These results indicate that for aqueous exposures resistance across the ABL at the gill surface, not the epithelial membrane itself, may be the dominant diffusional barrier. Sensitivity of aqueous diffusion of free PFAA was almost 100% responsible for Pgill, suggesting that diffusion of free PFAA across the ABL is likely the rate-limiting step for overall mass transport across the gills.

Under the tested conditions, DOC-mediated transport across the ABL had a minor influence on modeled results. NSCs for PFAA partitioning to DOC (KDOC/w) and DOC concentrations in laboratory water (CDOC) were generally between −0.001% and −0.7% for BCFs, and up to −1.0% for half-lives (PFUDA). These effects were measurable only for long-chain PFAA and remained small compared to ABL diffusion and tissue binding. Our results agree with earlier models for hydrophobic organic contaminants, where DOC sorption reduces freely dissolved contaminant concentrations and affects overall mass transport when hydrophobicity and DOC levels are both high.31,32

### Influence of environmental factors on BCFs

To assess changes in BCFs under environmentally relevant conditions, we varied each parameter individually, holding all others constant. Model simulations revealed that changes in ABL thickness following changes in water flow and high aqueous DOC concentration can influence PFAA BCFs. DOC was predicted to have minimal impact in typical freshwater environments (Tables S6 and S7). Comparing flow-through conditions, which yielded an ABL thickness of 0.016 cm, to static conditions with an ABL of 0.082 cm,50 median BCFs decreased by <0.01–26%, with the largest effects observed for short-chain PFAA (Tables S6 and S7). Similar findings have been reported for highly hydrophobic compounds, where ABL diffusion in internal compartments such as the gastrointestinal tract can limit uptake.62

DOC-related parameters exhibited low sensitivity overall (NSC < ±0.1%), yet BCFs decreased by up to 22% at elevated DOC concentrations (CDOC = 1 × 10−4 g mL−1). Reductions in BCFs correlated with the log KOC of the compounds (1.51–4.20). This result is consistent with previous models that predicted lower uptake of superhydrophobic compounds due to reductions in freely dissolved, bioavailable concentrations in the water phase.27 Large reductions in BCFs are not expected under typical ranges of environmental DOC levels.49,63 For PFAA with log KOC < 3, BCFs changed by less than 2%. Under the modified laboratory test setting, PFUDA (log KOC = 4.20) decreased by only 12%, likely due to constant influx sustaining the free aqueous concentration and enhancing DOC-mediated transport. These findings suggest that using a standard laboratory setting in BCF tests (i.e., single PFAA spike) could underestimate the bioconcentration potential of long-chain PFAA with high affinity for organic matter in natural water sources (i.e., constant PFAA influx) with high DOC content (e.g., swamp waters >30 mg L−1).63

### Distribution of PFAA among fish tissues

Across the seven tissues in the model, blood contained the largest mass fraction of PFAA but not the highest concentration (Fig. S2). Compartments such as the gills and kidneys exceeded blood concentrations but accounted for lower total mass due to their smaller volumes. These rankings are not directly comparable with reported field concentrations, which are usually measured in plasma or serum and account for 40–50% of whole blood in fish.64 Modeled whole-blood values reported here are correspondingly lower. Tissue-to-blood ratios above one for several PFAA are consistent with aqueous-exposure distribution studies.65 Because tissue partitioning was identified as one of the primary drivers of BCFs and elimination half-lives, we further examined the distribution of PFAA across individual fish tissues. We modeled the PFAA distribution across six tissues following aqueous exposures of 28 days in the gills, liver, kidneys, muscle, adipose, and rest-of-body (Fig. 4). Muscle accounted for the largest fraction of total PFAA body burden (14–84%) due to its large volume (47% of body mass), despite comparatively lower concentrations. Highest concentrations were simulated in the kidneys, followed by the gills and liver, with lower levels in adipose, muscle, and the “rest” compartment. Tissue mass fractions followed the order: muscle > gills > kidneys > liver > adipose > rest. Concentrations were highest in the kidneys and gills, intermediate in liver and adipose, and lowest in muscle and “rest” of the body. PFUDA deviated from this pattern, exhibiting both a high muscle burden and elevated adipose concentrations.

For short-chain PFAA (ηpfc < 7), kidney concentrations were highest, followed by the gills and liver. Concentrations in the gills were 1.2–1.3-fold higher than in the liver and 25–50-fold higher than in muscle. For example, PFHxS concentrations in the gills were 1.2× higher than the liver, 1.2× lower than in kidney, and over 60× higher than in muscle. Sub-compartment modeling indicated that PFAA predominantly bind to functional proteins (73–99% of total PFAA in gills), followed by structural proteins (0.48–14%) and phospholipids (0.28–12%) (Fig. S3). This distribution pattern likely reflects the high total protein content (20%) of gills, including functional (4.1%) and structural proteins (16%), as well as phospholipids (0.23%),48 in combination with binding affinities of PFAA to functional proteins (log KFP/W = 3.3–4.9), structural proteins (log KSP/W = 0.64–3.6), and phospholipids (log KPL/W = 2.3–5.2). These results suggest that binding to proteins and phospholipids in the gills is a major driver of PFAA bioaccumulation in fish. This is particularly relevant for compounds with shorter perfluorinated chain lengths (ηpfc < 7), which, in this case study, deposited over 20% of the total body burden in the gills.

### Implications for laboratory and field bioaccumulation studies

Our findings have several implications for interpreting PFAS bioaccumulation data and for improving food-web modeling frameworks. For long-chain PFAA (ηpfc > 7), tissue binding dominated BCFs, indicating that bioconcentration is primarily governed by tissue composition, particularly protein and phospholipid content. Given equal aqueous PFAA exposures, BCF values are likely to be more sensitive to interspecies differences in tissue composition across habitats and evolutionary branches relative to hydrodynamic conditions. In contrast, short-chain PFAA (ηpfc < 7) exhibited greater sensitivity to gill permeability, specifically transport across the ABL, indicating that processes affecting ABL thickness, such as water flow, mixing, and ventilation rates, may substantially influence uptake and depuration. This mechanistic distinction likely explains the higher variability observed in laboratory BCF measurements for short-chain PFAS8 and underscores the importance of standardizing turbulence and flow conditions across experimental systems.

Classical food-web models that represent bioaccumulation as an equilibrium partitioning process are likely to capture long-chain PFAS behavior when tissue binding is parameterized for protein- and phospholipid-rich tissues rather than neutral storage lipids alone.19 However, such models are insufficient for short-chain PFAS (ηpfc < 7) because uptake is strongly controlled by gill-mediated transport and hydrodynamic conditions. Accumulation of short-chain PFAA may be lower in environmental settings with low water movement and thick ABLs, such as lentic systems or sheltered bays compared to well-mixed rivers or coastal waters, whereas long-chain PFAS bioaccumulation remains largely insensitive to flow and is instead driven mainly by tissue composition.

Environmental drivers of PFAA bioaccumulation have historically received limited attention beyond pH effects.16 The TK model developed here highlights tissue binding and gill transport as important rate-limiting processes governing PFAS uptake and depuration, with the relative importance of each strongly dependent on fluorinated carbon chain length. Results show that effective gill permeability is largely controlled by ABL diffusion of freely dissolved and DOC-bound PFAA in waters rich in organic matter, emphasizing the need to account for both species-specific tissue composition and aqueous conditions such as flow regime and DOC concentrations. For example, marine species exhibit thinner blood–water diffusion distances at secondary lamellae than freshwater species such as perch,66 which may contribute to differences in uptake efficiency. Future models could incorporate the “leaky” nature of gill epithelia, including the role of tight junctions and associated proteins, which remain understudied.67

The model does not account for feedback between PFAS exposure and tissue composition, which may further modify bioaccumulation. Recent work showed that PFOA exposure can upregulate specific phospholipid subclasses in zebrafish liver,68 potentially increasing hepatic binding capacity for PFAA. Although PBTK models typically assume homogeneous tissue compartments,42,43 distribution within a tissue can be heterogeneous, reflecting regional differences in perfusion, membrane permeability, and binding.69–72 Resolving tissues at finer spatial resolution could improve the model for larger fish, where internal distribution is more likely to limit BCFs. In addition, large uncertainty in DOC binding, often parameterized as a function of KOW with confidence intervals spanning orders of magnitude, remains a key limitation for predicting PFAS uptake in DOC-rich systems.73 We used humic substances as a proxy for DOC,49 reflecting the allochthonous organic matter that dominates typical freshwater systems. However, DOC composition varies across systems, and autochthonous organic matter from phytoplankton, macrophytes, and microbial production is also important.74 Extending the model to these systems will require new data on PFAA partition coefficients for diverse types of DOC. Finally, conventional regulatory bioconcentration tests may fail to capture environmentally relevant exposure dynamics or critical life stages. The model simulates respiratory uptake of individual PFAA. Future extensions could add other exposure routes, such as dietary uptake, which becomes more important for longer-chain PFAA, as indicated in previous work.7 The model developed in this study only simulates exposure to terminal PFAA, but precursors such as perfluoroalkyl sulfonamides (FASA) can biotransform to terminal PFSA75 and, where present, can be important determinants of tissue concentrations. Representing precursor uptake would require additional data on biotransformation in the liver and gut and addition of such processes to the model. Mechanistic models such as the one presented here can help guide experimental design and improve alignment between laboratory bioaccumulation tests and real-world aqueous and biological conditions across ecosystems by explicitly incorporating hydrodynamics, aqueous conditions, and tissue composition.

## Current AI Paradigms

Before exploring the future of AI in veterinary medicine, we direct the reader’s attention to the area of animal behavior analysis in scientific research where AI is making a significant impact.

Animal behavior analysis is crucial across di­ verse scientific disciplines, including ecology, ethol­ ogy, and behavioral neuroscience.11–13 For example, when neuroscientists study the brain circuitry that regulates animal behavior, they need to define and categorize actions from large amounts of recorded behavioral videos. Manual analysis is prohibitively expensive with rapidly increasing amounts of data. However, automating this process is challenging because different laboratories study different be­ haviors, with different definitions, using different

experimental designs.11,14 We will discuss research in the direction of scientist-in-the-loop AI systems toward tackling these challenges.5,15,16 These sys­ tems are developed in collaboration with neurosci­ entists and computer scientists, in order to trans­ form diverse and complex experimental data into interpretable representations.

A comprehensive review of tools for behavior quantification can be found in a few other works.4,11,14 This section will focus specifically on the impact of 3 different AI paradigms on method development and deployment: supervised learning, self-supervised learning, and foundation models (Figure 1).

Supervised learning

Supervised learning is a widely used paradigm in animal behavior analysis. These methods have en­ abled researchers to automate the process of identi­ fying and categorizing behaviors from vast amounts of data. This approach relies on large, human-anno­ tated datasets to train models. During training, the model is exposed to many examples (like a student studying many cases) and learns to perform a spe­ cific task or group of tasks, such as identifying dif­ ferent behaviors from video recordings. The model learns the task by adjusting its internal parameters to improve its performance.

Once trained, these models can be applied to new, unseen data, similar to how a veterinarian ap­ plies their knowledge to diagnose new patients. However, the model’s performance on new data de­ pends on its ability to generalize: to apply what it has learned to different situations. For example, it would be difficult for an AI model trained only on videos of mice to accurately analyze the behavior of birds, or even for models trained only on videos of mice from one laboratory to generalize to mice from a dif­ ferent laboratory. In this case, the AI model may re­ quire fine-tuning to adjust to data that differ from its original training set. This fine-tuning involves further refining the model’s internal parameters to better match the characteristics of the new data.

The ability to generalize effectively often depends on the size and diversity of the original training dataset. A model trained on a wide range of behaviors, species, and experimental setups is more likely to generalize better to new and varied data. Therefore, before using an AI model in your workflow, it’s crucial to understand the type of data on which it was trained and evaluate it on your own data. This will help you assess whether the model is suitable for your specific needs or requires further adaptation.

One example of supervised learning in animal be­ havior analysis is the Mouse Action Recognition System (MARS),3 a collaborative effort between behavioral neu­ roscientists and computer scientists. The MARS tackles the challenge of automating behavior analysis by first requiring human experts to annotate video data. This process involves labeling anatomical landmarks (also called keypoints) on the animal’s body, such as the nose, tail, and paws. A model is then trained with the use of human annotations to detect these keypoints on new images; this task is called pose estimation, in which pose refers to the overall configuration of the body defined by keypoints. The next step requires users to assign be­ havioral labels to different video segments, like sniffing, grooming, or mounting. The model then learns to recog­ nize these behaviors by matching the visual information (keypoints and movement patterns) to the human-pro­ vided labels. This workflow of first performing pose es­ timation, then behavior classification is common across supervised learning setups and has also been reviewed in multiple works.4,11,17 Notably, tools for pose estima­ tion include DeepLabCut18 and SLEAP,19 which has been applied to label keypoints on species including flies and gerbils, as well as to track multiple animals in videos. Other tools for behavior classification include SimBA20 and DeepEthogram,21 in which the goal is to map each input video frame to a human-defined behavior label.

While supervised learning has significantly advanced the field of animal behavior analysis, several key challenges remain. (1) Annotation bottleneck: these models require a labeled training set to learn new tasks. Creating large, ac­ curately annotated datasets is time-consuming and expen­ sive, often requiring significant manual effort from experts, which limits the scalability of supervised learning approach­ es. For example, MARS is developed with approximately 14 hours of frame-level behavior annotations, and 15,000 frames of pose annotations across training and evaluation data. Researchers are exploring various techniques to ad­ dress this challenge, including active learning, transfer learning, and semi-supervised learning. (2) Generalization to new data: supervised learning models trained on a sin­ gle dataset may not generalize well to new datasets with different experimental setups, animal strains, or behavioral definitions. This is because the model might have learned features that are specific to the training dataset that don’t transfer well to new situations. For example, the MARS pose estimators were trained with images from a top-view cam­ era, and retraining with new data was needed for camera angles from the side. Additionally, the model was initially trained with black and white mice and might not general­ ize well to other colors or species. This highlights a com­ mon challenge in supervised learning: models often need to be adapted to new settings or types of data. Techniques to tackle this include transfer learning via fine-tuning, as well as data augmentation, which artificially increases the diversity of training data. (3) Interpretability: many

powerful models are complex ‘black boxes’ due to their ar­ chitectures and large numbers of parameters.17,22 This can make it difficult for researchers to trust the model’s output and gain insights into the underlying factors driving animal behavior. Researchers are actively developing techniques to make AI models more interpretable, such as highlight­ ing important features that influence decisions or iden­ tifying representative examples that activate specific model components.

Self-supervised learning

While supervised learning has been impactful,4,11,17 it often faces limitations due to the reliance on labeled data. Self-supervised learning23 offers an alternative approach by leveraging the inherent structure of the data itself to generate supervisory signals, eliminating the need for explicit labels. In self-supervised learn­ ing,24 pretext tasks are designed to encourage the model to learn relevant representations from unlabeled data without relying on explicit labels. These pretext tasks include predicting missing parts of the data or reconstructing the original data from a scrambled ver­ sion. These tasks enable the model to learn important features and relationships within the data without la­ bels (eg, training the model to predict future trajecto­ ries5), which can then be used for other downstream tasks (eg, using the learned representation as input for behavior classification). The performance of a self-su­ pervised model is often judged by how well it performs on a separate task, like accurately classifying different behaviors, after it has learned from the unlabeled data.

One example of a self-supervised framework for studying behavior is task programming,5 which uses pre­ text tasks designed by experts to learn representations of behavior in a self-supervised way, in addition to predict­ ing future trajectories. These tasks represent attributes important for studying behavior, such as the distance be­ tween animals or speed of each animal. This encourages the model to learn about spatial and temporal relation­ ships in trajectory data, as well as important features of animal behavior defined by experts. Once trained, these representations can be applied to learn human-defined behaviors with significant reduction in annotation re­ quirements. Other frameworks for self-supervised learn­ ing of behavior are reviewed in Luxem et al4 and notably includes VAME,25 which uses a variational autoencoder to map trajectory data to a lower dimensional space and perform clustering for behavior discovery. Instead of be­ havior, another line of work15,26 uses self-supervised learn­ ing to discover keypoints from behavioral videos. B-KinD trains a model to reconstruct the movements in the origi­ nal video (eg, difference across 2 video frames) in order to enable the model to learn meaningful representations of the animal’s body and movement, even without explicit keypoint annotations. Finally, there are also frameworks that use unsupervised learning,27 which learns structure from data without a pretext task.

One of the key advantages of self-supervised learning is its ability to leverage large amounts of unla­ beled data,24 which is more readily available compared to expert-labeled data. This makes these techniques especially valuable in veterinary medicine, in which labeled data for diverse animal species, complex pa­ tient records, and varied imaging modalities (eg, ra­ diographs, ultrasounds, histopathology) can be scarce

Foundation models

Building on advances in self-supervised learning, foundation models represent a recent paradigm shift in AI.28 These models are trained on massive, diverse datasets, often encompassing internet-scale data. During training, foundation models use self-super­ vised objectives that enable them to learn represen­ tations without explicit labels across massive datas­ ets. This allows them to be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks with minimal or no fine-tuning. A prominent example29 is large language models like GPT-4, which has demonstrated a wide range of capa­ bilities in natural language understanding and genera­ tion after being trained on vast amounts of text data. This represents a departure from self-supervised methods discussed in the previous section in terms of training data scale, general-purpose nature of the learned model, and emergent capabilities.

In the domain of video analysis, foundation mod­ els are also emerging as a promising tool.30–32 One example, which has been applied to animal behavior analysis, is VideoPrism,33 a video foundation model trained on a massive dataset of approximately 600 million videos. VideoPrism is a video encoder that maps input videos to semantically meaningful rep­ resentations, which then empower a range of down­ stream tasks in computer vision, including captioning, video question answering, and video-text retrieval. In addition, this model, with minimal adaptation, is applicable to a variety of animal behavior analysis tasks,34 including localization, behavior classification, and retrieval of videos with similar behaviors.

Training and developing foundation models is a computationally intensive process that requires signifi­ cant resources and expertise (eg, estimation for a sin­ gle training run of a 1.5 billion–parameter model is at least $80,000, depending on factors such as hardware, dataset size, and training time).35 For example, these models often contain a large number of parameters (eg, a 70 billion–parameter open-sourced language

model36) to fit the massive training datasets. How­ ever, once trained, these models can be readily used by researchers and practitioners without the need for extensive model training or fine-tuning.28 This provides researchers in animal behavior with access to powerful AI systems that could potentially work out of the box on their data. These general-purpose capabilities also hold promise for applications in veterinary medicine, such as analyzing patient videos, predicting disease risk, and assisting with clinical decision-making.

Furthermore, foundation models provide a strong starting point for specialization. Domain-specific mod­ els can be derived from foundation models through finetuning on smaller, targeted datasets.28 In the future, a foundation model trained on diverse animal videos could be further fine-tuned on a dataset of videos specifically focused on canine behavior to improve its performance on canine-specific tasks. Alternatively, a decoder mod­ ule, which translates the general representations learned by the foundation model into task-specific outputs, can be added to adapt it to specific tasks or datasets. Vid­ eoPrism, originally trained on internet videos, learns a general-purpose video representation that is compat­ ible with various decoders (eg, classification or localiza­ tion) for animal behavior analysis.34 In a similar fashion, it is also possible to train decoders to identify specific diseases or conditions from general-purpose video foundation model representations.

## Future Opportunities and Challenges

The AI paradigms discussed in the previous sec­ tion—supervised, self-supervised, and foundation models—each present unique opportunities and chal­ lenges for animal behavior analysis as well as veteri­ nary medicine. While the current focus in the field is on leveraging large-scale datasets to train generaliz­ able models, several challenges remain. Here, we dis­ cuss key challenges related to data, model develop­ ment, and evaluation, focusing on their implications for users of AI systems in veterinary practice. As the field of AI rapidly evolves, it is crucial to proactively anticipate and address these emerging opportunities and challenges to ensure the responsible and effec­ tive integration of new technologies into veterinary medicine. Readers interested in a more comprehen­ sive discussion of the evolving regulatory landscape and ethical frameworks for AI in veterinary medicine are referred to recent reviews on this topic.1,9,10

Data

For modern AI models to generalize to unseen settings (eg, new clinics, new patients, new tasks), they require large, diverse training datasets. There is an opportunity to pool datasets containing hetero­ geneous data modalities, such as electronic health records, medical images (x-rays, ultrasounds, etc), pathology reports, genomic sequences, and even sensor data from wearable devices, across various sources, such as veterinary hospitals, research insti­ tutions, and diagnostic laboratories. However, data sharing and aggregation raise important questions about data ownership, privacy, security, and usage rights. Finally, because the performance of AI systems is highly dependent on their training data, practitio­ ners and users should be aware of the data on which the model they are using is trained (or have a way to evaluate the model carefully in their setting) before deploying it in clinical practice.

Model

The diverse range of data modalities and tasks in veterinary medicine—from radiographs and blood­ work to clinical notes and genomic data—presents a unique opportunity to push the capabilities of modern AI systems. However, this also presents a challenge: effectively integrating these diverse data types into a cohesive, interpretable system. For ex­ ample, imagine a computational system that can analyze a radiograph; cross-reference it with the pa­ tient’s breed, age, and clinical history; and then sug­ gest a diagnosis while also providing the reasoning behind its conclusion, drawing on established veteri­ nary knowledge and best practices. To achieve this, we need models that not only leverage the power of deep learning on large datasets but also incorpo­ rate decades of accumulated veterinary expertise. This human-in-the-loop approach, in which AI learns from and collaborates with veterinarians, is crucial not only for improving animal care but also for build­ ing trust in these systems.

One step toward this approach is to develop models that can explain their reasoning in a way that is meaningful to veterinarians. Veterinary medi­ cine encompasses a wide range of specialties, each with its own unique knowledge base and clinical focus. For instance, an explanation of patient conditions and diagnosis might vary for a radiologist, oncologist, or cardiologist. To achieve this, close collaboration be­ tween AI researchers and veterinary professionals

is crucial. By working together, we can ensure that these models are developed and deployed in a way that addresses the specific needs, concerns, and ethical considerations of the veterinary community. This collaboration can help bridge the gap between computational expertise and domain-specific knowl­ edge, leading to more effective and trustworthy AI solutions for veterinary medicine.

Finally, there is an opportunity to enhance the human-animal bond by providing tools to continu­ ously monitor and analyze animal behavior, com­ munication, and emotional states from videos, wear­ ables, or other devices. This can lead to improved response to the needs of animals (eg, improving live­ stock health39,40) as well as a strengthened connec­ tion between humans and their animal companions. For example, AI-powered apps could provide per­ sonalized recommendations for pet care and train­ ing, tailored to the specific needs and personality of the animal. However, it’s important to consider how the technology is used in a way that complements, not replaces, human-animal interactions.

Evaluation

Evaluating the impact of AI on animal well-be­ ing is crucial but complex, requiring a multifaceted approach that goes beyond traditional metrics like accuracy.41 While AI offers promising applications in continuous monitoring, early disease detection, and personalized interventions, assessing its true impact on animal welfare can be challenging. To tackle this challenge, we need to develop robust evaluation metrics that capture the multifaceted aspects of ani­ mal well-being, including the following: (1) physical health indicators such as recovery time, longevity, and disease rate and (2) behavioral and emotional state indicators such as social interactions, vocaliza­ tions, and signs of stress. In addition, we also need metrics to assess how AI impacts the veterinary practice itself, such as client and veterinarian satis­ faction, diagnostic accuracy, and efficiency.

Furthermore, establishing standardized pro­ tocols for data collection and evaluation facilitates comparability across different studies, enabling us to better measure the progress of model develop­ ment in the field. This is particularly crucial as the field moves toward more collaborative and open research. Notable examples of standardization ef­ fort from other fields include data sheets for docu­ menting data collection and usage from machine learning42; the Neurodata Without Borders format, introduced for organizing and sharing neurophysiol­ ogy data43; and guidelines for using and developing open-source tools for behavioral video analysis (such as the use of large-scale standardized benchmarks).4 In human medicine, large-scale datasets with stan­ dardized formats have enabled the development of powerful models for language (eg, Med-PaLM44) and medical image segmentation (eg, Med-SAM45).

## Call for Collaborations

As AI’s impact on veterinary medicine grows, we stand at a crossroads. Will AI-powered tools work with veterinarians to improve animal health world­ wide and enable new ways for humans and animals to connect? Or will the rise of commercial AI systems exacerbate existing challenges, potentially influenc­ ing shortages in the veterinary workforce, impacting human expertise, increasing stress, and disrupting work-life balance? Will these algorithms ultimately help or hinder the practice of veterinary medicine and the connection between humans and animals? The choices we make today will shape the future of veterinary medicine for years to come.

To ensure a future in which AI benefits all, we must actively forge a path of responsible develop­ ment and deployment. This requires a collaborative effort, bringing together diverse perspectives and expertise (Figure 2): • Datasets and benchmarks: The trajectory of AI is shaped not only by researchers but also by the availability of high-quality data and bench­ marks. To develop AI for all, we need diverse and representative datasets that encompass a wide range of animal species, breeds, ages, health conditions, and geographic locations. This en­ ables us to develop models that generalize well across populations and clinical settings and help

mitigate bias (eg, overrepresentation of certain species such as cats and dogs). Furthermore, establishing clear data ownership and shar­ ing agreements is crucial when building these datasets. To encourage wider participation, open data initiatives could be considered, but we need to carefully balance the benefits of data sharing with the need to protect patient privacy and confidentiality. Finally, developing standard­ ized benchmarks and evaluation metrics will al­ low for more fair comparisons between different AI models and facilitate progress in the field. • Domain expertise: Decades of accumulated hu­ man expertise already exist in veterinary medi­ cine. Integrating AI systems with this knowledge requires a multifaceted approach. First, humanin-the-loop systems can empower veterinarians to actively participate in the entire model lifecycle, from model development and deployment to on­ going evaluation. This can involve providing feed­ back on model predictions, improving existing al­ gorithms, and contributing training data. Second, we need human-interpretable models to enable bidirectional knowledge transfer. This is an active area with works in explainable AI and machine learning,46 mechanistic interpretability,47 and neu­ rosymbolic modeling.16,48 Further research in these areas enables veterinarians to both integrate their domain expertise into the model and extract new insights and knowledge from the model’s outputs. # Clinical characterization of Aqueous and Vitreous Retinol Binding Protein 3 (RBP3) Concentrations in Relation to Diabetic Retinopathy Severity, Retinal Structures, and Systemic Complications

**Authors:** Ward Fickweiler; Tanvi Chokshi; Surya Jangolla; Margalit Mitzner; I-Hsien Wu; Hyunseok Park; Kyoungmin Park; Lloyd Paul Aiello; Jennifer Sun; George L. King

## Abstract

To evaluate Retinol Binding Protein 3 (RBP3) from photoreceptors in aqueous and its association to vitreous, diabetic retinopathy (DR) severity, retinal layer thickness and clinical characteristics in people with diabetes.

RBP3 concentration was measured by custom-developed ELISA assay in aqueous and correlated to vitreous concentrations in patients from the 50-Year Medalist Study and Beetham Eye Institute at Joslin Diabetes Center.

Aqueous RBP3 concentration (N=131) was elevated in eyes with no to mild DR (mean ± SD 0.7nM ± 0.2) and decreased in eyes with moderate to severe DR (0.65nM ± 0.3) and proliferative DR (PDR, 0.5nM ± 0.2, P<0.001) compared to eyes without diabetes. Aqueous and vitreous RBP3 concentrations correlated with each other (r=0.34, P=0.001) and between fellow eyes (P<0.0001). History of retinal surgery did not affect aqueous RBP3 concentrations, but cataract surgery affected both vitreous and aqueous levels. Elevated aqueous RBP3 concentration associated with increased thickness of outer nuclear layer (P=0.004) and correlated with HbA1c, whereas vitreous RBP3 correlated with diabetic systemic complications.

These findings suggest that aqueous RBP3 concentration may be an important an endogenous clinical retinal protective factor, a biomarker for DR severity, and a promising VEGF-independent clinical intervention target in diabetic retinopathy.

## Abstract

Aqueous RBP3 concentration is inversely correlated with DR severity, lower than vitreous concentration, and corresponds to neural retinal layer thicknesses, suggesting it may be a novel clinically useful retinal protective factor and biomarker for DR.

## Introduction

Diabetic retinopathy (DR) occurs in a majority of patients with 20 years or more of diabetes despite aggressive control of systemic risk factors1. Although laser photocoagulation and anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents are effective treatments for vision-threatening complications of proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR)2,3, interventions other than glycemic control that target the toxic effects of hyperglycemia in the retina have not been successful in delaying or preventing the initiation and progression of early stages of non-proliferative DR4. Thus, there is an important need to identify new clinically relevant biomarkers and therapeutic interventional targets for early stages of DR.

Findings from the Joslin 50-Year Medalist cohort, a group composed of individuals who have had insulin-dependent diabetes for 50 years or longer, have provided strong clinical support that endogenous retinal protective factors exist5–8 which can counteract the toxic effects of hyperglycemia5, and reduce the risk of advanced diabetic retinopathy6. Previously, we reported that photoreceptor-secreted Retinol Binding Protein 3 (RBP3, interstitial retinoid-binding protein) was found to be significantly elevated in comparative proteomic analysis of retina from those protected from DR even with extreme chronic duration of hyperglycemia compared to those with severe DR or PDR9. RBP3’s protective actions were shown to be mediated by inhibiting hyperglycemia’s toxic effects on the expression of inflammatory cytokines and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) in the retina7. Increased expression of RBP3 targeted to the photoreceptors or by intravitreal injections were shown to prevent DR lesions in rodent models of DR6. These exciting studies have identified the first neuroretinal selective protein to act on retinal vasculature to prevent DR progression, suggesting therapeutic and diagnostic possibilities for patients with diabetes independent of current therapeutic modalities.

There is emerging interest in the identification of proteins in aqueous fluid related to DR due to its easier access, relatively low risk of complications10,11,and minimal trauma to the eye compared to vitreous sampling12. Liquid biopsy of aqueous fluid has been useful in the management of ocular tumors13 and uveitis, and may also have relevance in DR. Proteomic studies have identified several potential DR biomarkers in the aqueous, which include inflammatory cytokines14, 15. However, a major limiting factor for the usefulness of those factors is that they are expressed mostly in other tissues. Thus, aqueous and vitreous levels of those factors may not specifically represent retinal changes. In contrast, RBP3 is overwhelmingly expressed in the photoreceptors, with only very minor expression in the pineal gland. Thus, changes in RBP3 concentration in ocular fluids such as vitreous and aqueous would likely reflect changes and severity in the retina as we have previously reported in vitreous6,7. RBP3 concentrations, however, have not been measured in aqueous fluid nor correlated with vitreous RBP3 concentration and DR severity clinically. One limiting factor has been the availability of a sensitive and specific and quantitative assay for RBP3 to detect the much lower concentrations found in the aqueous. In this study, we developed a custom ELISA assay that can detect and quantitatively measure RBP3 concentrations in aqueous fluid. This assay allows for the first characterization of a retinal selective protein (RBP3) between aqueous and vitreous, and its association with diabetic retinopathy severity, retinal cell layers, and systemic complications. These studies thus provide data characterizing this molecule as a retinal specific biomarker for severity of DR and potential therapeutic intervention for diabetic retinal disease.

## Research Samples and Methods

### Samples and Study Design

This is an observational retrospective study that included all available postmortem aqueous and vitreous samples from individuals in the Medalist study, additional aqueous and vitreous surgical samples from those who underwent ocular surgeries and aqueous samples from people with type 1 or 2 diabetes who underwent cataract surgery from 2011 to 2015 at the Beetham Eye Institute (BEI) of the Joslin Diabetes Center. Informed consent was obtained from all Medalist participants. The Joslin institutional review board approved the Medalist components of the study, and the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center institutional review boards approved the discarded surgical samples portion of the study. The postmortem and surgical samples were analyzed together. Clinical characteristics were collected through structured chart review at the Joslin Diabetes Center from the BEI and the Medalist Study. Laboratory metrics were also collected including HbA1c. Laboratory values were obtained from those available closest to collection of the aqueous sample. Diabetic retinopathy was graded using the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study severity scale. Individual retinal layer thicknesses in the foveal 1×1mm area were measured by spectral domain optical coherence tomography with automated layer segmentation software (SPECTRALIS v6.0; Heidelberg Engineering, Heidelberg, Germany).

### ELISA Assay

Luminescence enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) protocol was optimized from Yokomizo et al6 for the quantification of RBP3 within the aqueous. In brief, changes from this protocol included the use of a custom designed polyclonal anti-RBP3 antibody targeted human RBP3 and made with Vivitide (8ug/mL) for capture and a custom designed monoclonal biotinylated anti-RBP3 antibody made against human RBP3 (3ug/mL, Vivitide) for detection. The negative controls were bovine serum albumin (BSA), immunoglobulin G (IgG), and retinol-binding protein 4 (RBP4). BSA, IgG, and RBP4 concentrations were measured using an ELISA kit (R&D systems, MN, USA). All concentrations of negative controls tested were in the range of physiological concentrations of the protein in the aqueous (BSA: 3.0μM; IgG: 0.7μM; RBP4: 1.0nM)16,17.

### Statistical Analyses

Statistical analyses were performed using SAS, version 9.4. Descriptive statistics are presented as mean (± SD), median (interquartile range), or frequencies, as appropriate. Generalized estimating equations with an unstructured correlation matrix were employed to assess the cross-sectional relationships between aqueous RBP3 outcomes and systemic and ocular clinical characteristics. This method was adjusted for within-subject correlations as each patient had 2 unique values per eye. Models were adjusted for relevant clinical based on a priori knowledge and bivariate analyses to control for confounding factors, as described in the legends of the figures.

## Results

### Patient and ocular characteristics

Clinical characteristics of all subjects with available aqueous samples (N=129, Table 1) showed mean (+/− SD) age 73.2 ± 7.9 years, disease duration 56 ± 15 years, A1C 7.3 ± 1.0%, body mass index (BMI) 26 ± 4.3, systolic blood pressure (SBP) 134 ± 19 mmHg, diastolic blood pressure (DBP) 63 ± 9 mmHg, and total cholesterol 154 ± 36 mg/dL. Ocular characteristics (N=129 eyes, Table 1) of this cohort showed 71.2% with history of cataract surgery, 32% with no to mild DR and 41% with PDR.

### RBP3 Detection in All Aqueous Samples

Our custom-developed ELISA assay detected RBP3 concentrations in all aqueous samples (N=131) that were collected from people with type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Once diluted 10-fold, all aqueous samples fell within a 0.3–0.8nM range with the mean concentration of the samples being 0.6±0.2nM (Supplemental Figure 1). IgG, RBP4, and BSA, at protein concentrations of 0.7μM, 1.0nM, and 3.0 μM, respectively, were not detected by the ELISA assay confirming specificity for detection of RBP3 (Supplemental Figure 2). Linearity-of-dilution assay included 2, 3, and 4-fold dilutions with a mean recovery of 106% across samples (Supplemental Figure 3). Intra-assay correlation was R2 of 0.99 with average coefficient of variation of 13%.

### Elevated Aqueous RBP3 Associated with Milder DR

Increasing aqueous RBP3 concentration was associated with decreasing DR severity (Figure 1A). RBP3 concentrations were measured in those with no diabetes, no to mild DR, moderate to severe DR, and PDR. There was an increase in aqueous RBP3 concentration in eyes with no to mild DR (P=0.02) compared to eyes with no diabetes (0.56±0.19nM). Aqueous RBP3 concentrations decreased from 0.7 ± 0.2nM in eyes with no to mild DR to 0.5 ± 0.2nM in eyes with PDR (P<0.001). Similarly, there was a decrease in RBP3 concentrations between eyes with moderate to severe DR (0.65 ± 0.3nM) compared to eyes with PDR (P=0.01). For eyes with PDR, aqueous RBP3 concentrations from surgical (0.4 ± 0.2nM) samples were similar to postmortem Medalists (0.6 ± 0.2nM) samples (P=0.11).

### Positive Association of Aqueous RBP3 with Vitreous RBP3

There was a significant positive correlation (r=0.34, P=0.001) between RBP3 concentrations in aqueous and vitreous of paired eyes (N=91, Figure 1B). RBP3 concentrations were consistently higher in vitreous compared to aqueous samples. There was a 12-fold difference between mean vitreous (16.2 ± 21.3nM) and mean aqueous (0.6 ± 0.2nM) RBP3 concentrations.

### Association of Aqueous and Vitreous RBP3 with Systemic Clinical Characteristics

Unadjusted bivariate analysis with systemic characteristics showed that aqueous RBP3 concentration was inversely associated with HbA1c (β estimate (β) −0.07, 95% confidence interval (CI) −0.12;−0.02, P=0.01) and positively associated with age (β 0.01, 95% CI 0.001;0.01, P=0.01) (Table 2), whereas vitreous RBP3 concentrations were associated with age (β 0.028, 95% CI 0.008;0.048, P=0.01), but not with HbA1c (P=0.88) or duration of diabetes (P=0.18). Vitreous RBP3 concentrations were associated with nephropathy (β 11.5, 95% CI 2.5; 20.4, P=0.01) and inversely associated to albumin to creatinine ratio (β −0.01, 95% CI −0.01;−0.003, P=0.001), however aqueous RBP was not associated with either nephropathy (P=0.92) or albumin to creatinine ratio (P=0.11). Vitreous concentrations of RBP3 were higher in patients who had neuropathy (β 8.1, 95% CI 1.0;15.1, P=0.03), hypertension (β 11.5, 95% CI 7.3;19.2, P<0.0001), cardiac disease (β 11.8, 95% CI 6.3;17.3, P<0.0001), or high total cholesterol (β 13.0, 95% CI 6.6;19.4, P<0.0001), while aqueous RBP3 concentrations were not associated with neuropathy (P=0.10), hypertension (SBP P=0.58, DBP P=0.08), cardiac disease (P=0.04), or total cholesterol concentrations (P=0.32).

### Association of Aqueous and Vitreous RBP3 with Ocular Clinical Characteristics

In unadjusted analysis for ocular characteristics, aqueous and vitreous RBP3 concentrations were positively associated with history of prior cataract surgery (β 0.14, 95% CI 0.03; 0.26, P=0.01 and β 13.9, 95% CI 7.4; 20.3, P<0.0001, respectively). Vitreous RBP3 concentrations correlated inversely with history of intravitreal injections (β −15.7, 95% CI −26.9;−4.4, P=0.01), laser photocoagulation (β −9.3, 95% CI −21.9; 3.4, P=0.15) and vitrectomy (β −12.1, 95% CI −22.6; −1.7, P=0.02). However, these ocular procedures were not significantly associated with aqueous RBP3 concentrations (intravitreal injections P=0.84, laser photocoagulation P=0.92, vitrectomy P=0.71). In multivariable analyses adjusting for all significant systemic and ocular variables in unadjusted analyses, DR severity remained significantly associated with RBP3 in both aqueous (no-mild DR v. PDR, β 0.15, 95% CI 0.06; 0.23, P=0.001, Figure 2A) and vitreous fluid (β 36.2, 95% CI 5.7; 66.6, P=0.02, Figure 2B).

### Aqueous and Vitreous RBP3 Correlation between Paired Eyes

Aqueous RBP3 concentrations (mean 0.7±0.2nM) were also available from the fellow eye in 47 patients (94 eyes, Figure 3A). There was a strong positive correlation (r=0.65, P<0.0001) of aqueous RBP3 concentrations between fellow eyes (right eye mean 0.7±0.2nM, left eye mean 0.6±0.2nM). Vitreous RBP3 concentrations were measured from fellow eyes in 34 patients (68 eyes, Figure 3B) where there was a strong positive correlation in vitreous RBP3 concentrations (r=0.86, P<0.0001).

### Association of Retinal Layer Thicknesses with Aqueous RBP3

Elevated aqueous RBP3 concentrations were associated with increased thickness of the outer nuclear layer (Figure 4, ONL, β estimate (β) 0.01, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.002;0.004, P=0.004), outer plexiform layer (OPL β 0.02, 95% CI 0.004;0.04, P=0.02), and inner plexiform layer (IPL β 0.01, 95% CI 0.001; 0.02, P=0.02) and thinning of the retinal pigment epithelial layer (RPE, β −0.006, CI −0.01;0.01, P=0.01). There was no significant association between aqueous RBP3 concentration and other individual retinal layer thicknesses, including RNFL (P= 0.60), GCL (P=0.15), and INL (P=0.11).

## Discussion

This study provides the first quantitative analysis of aqueous RBP3 concentration relative to its levels in the vitreous, with respect to severity of DR and with other ocular and systemic clinical characteristics. Such data are supportive of potentially using RPB3 as a clinically important biomarker for diabetic retinal disease and further characterize its potential role as a therapeutic target. Using a custom developed ELISA assay with enhanced sensitivity, we were able to detect RBP3 concentrations in all aqueous samples and showed that it is significantly lower than found in vitreous. This is expected since RBP3 originates in the photoreceptors. The results indicated that higher concentrations of aqueous RBP3 are associated with protection from advanced DR, similar to the findings of vitreous RBP3 concentrations, supporting its potential usefulness as a biomarker for DR severity in people with diabetes.

The findings that both aqueous and vitreous RBP3 concentrations were highly correlated in the fellow eyes suggests that single eye sampling might be reflective of DR severity in both eyes. This is an important finding clinically since aqueous sampling is safer and more feasible for patients than vitreous biopsy. Similar to the vitreous, higher aqueous RBP3 concentration was associated with increased outer retinal layer thickness in people with diabetes, which is an important positive control marker, since thicker outer retinal layers have been reported in eyes with milder DR18. These findings suggest that higher RBP3 concentration may promote preservation of photoreceptor structure, thus preventing or slowing DR progression and also serving as a biomarker for such events.

Our prior studies suggest that retinal RBP3 may also have a protective effect against the progression of DR6. It is likely that RBP3 has multiple actions on various retinal cells besides its well-established and critical function of transporting retinols between photoreceptors and RPE or Muller cells19. Due to inhibition of glucose uptake, reduction of inflammation and VEGF expression, and increased regeneration of retinal cells6, several studies have suggested that RBP3 may delay or prevent the degeneration of retina. The loss of RBP3 by mutation or deletion results in retinal degeneration similar to that observed in retinitis pigmentosa19,20.

Our findings of elevated aqueous RBP3 concentrations in eyes with moderate to severe DR and no to mild DR compared to eyes with PDR are consistent with previous findings in vitreous and retina samples6,7. Slower progression to PDR is also seen in eyes with higher vitreous RBP3 concentration7. These data suggest that RBP3-based diagnostics by aqueous measurement may be helpful for clinicians in stratifying people with diabetes for risk of DR progression. Further longitudinal clinical studies of diverse patient populations tracking serial RBP3 concentrations in aqueous will be needed to determine the predictive value of RBP3 as a biomarker for people with diabetes.

There are limitations to this study. There was variable time between the OCT imaging and the time when the aqueous sample was collected, ranging from 2016–2022. Many of the samples came from postmortem specimens, but the associations were similar in fresh surgical samples as well. We would need a larger validation cohort, with both type 1 and type 2 patients, to provide adequate power to rigorously define differences between surgical and postmortem samples and assure the utility of fresh aqueous samples. We also recognize that statistical significance is not equivalent to clinical relevance and further studies are needed to better establish the magnitude and clinical utility of aqueous RBP3 measurement. In summary, aqueous RBP3 concentrations correlate with vitreous RBP3 concentrations and are inversely correlated to severity of DR. Due to the relative ease of accessibility, assays of aqueous RBP3 levels provides a promising clinically relevant biomarker for severity of DR and its progression, which could be useful for clinical research, development of new therapeutics, and clinical care for diabetic retinopathy.

## Abstract

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are a large class of highly fluorinated anthropogenic chemicals. Some PFAS bioaccumulate in aquatic food webs, thereby posing risks for seafood consumers. Existing models for persistent organic pollutants (POPs) perform poorly for ionizable PFAS. Here we adapt a well-established food web bioaccumulation model for neutral POPs to predict the bioaccumulation behavior of six perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAAs) and two perfluoroalkyl ether acids (HFPO-DA, 9-Cl-PF3ONS) produced as PFAA replacements. The new model includes sorption to blood plasma proteins and phospholipids, empirically parameterized membrane transport, and renal elimination for PFAAs. Improved performance relative to prior models without these updates is shown by comparing simulations to field and lab measurements. PFAS with eight or more perfluorinated carbons (ηpfc ≥ 8, i.e., C8 perfluorosulfonic acid, C10–C11 perfluorocarboxylic acid, 9-Cl-PF3ONS) are often the most abundant in aquatic food webs. The new model reproduces their observed bioaccumulation potential within a factor of two for >80% of fish species, indicating its readiness to support development of fish consumption advisories for these compounds. Results suggest bioaccumulation of ηpfc ≥ 8 PFAS is primarily driven by phospholipid partitioning, and that renal elimination is negligible for these compounds. However, specific protein binding mechanisms are important for reproducing the observed tissue concentrations of many shorter-chain PFAAs, including protein transporter-mediated renal elimination. Additional data on protein-binding and membrane transport mechanisms for PFAS are needed to better understand the biological behavior of shorter-chain PFAAs and their alternatives.
